metadata.title: Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

nodes.name: Quantum gate array
nodes.statement: A set of quantum gates with logical wires connecting their inputs and outputs; the input (with extra work bits set to $0$) is fed through a sequence of quantum gates and observed at the output.

nodes.name: Quantum state superposition
nodes.statement: A pure quantum state on $n$ bits is a unit-length vector $\sum_{i=0}^{2^n-1} a_i \| S_i \rangle$ in a $2^n$-dimensional Hilbert space, with $\sum_i |a_i|^2 = 1$.

nodes.name: Local unitary transformation
nodes.statement: A unitary transformation acting on a fixed (constant) number of bits; quantum circuits are restricted to compositions of such local gates so that they can be physically implemented.

nodes.name: BQP
nodes.statement: The class of functions computable in polynomial time on a quantum computer with bounded error probability; the quantum analogue of the classical class BPP.

nodes.name: Toffoli gate
nodes.statement: A reversible 3-bit gate (controlled-controlled-NOT) that negates the third bit if and only if the first two bits are $1$; universal for reversible classical computation.

nodes.name: Fredkin gate
nodes.statement: A reversible 3-bit gate that swaps the last two bits when the first bit is $0$ and leaves them untouched otherwise; universal for reversible classical computation.

nodes.name: Modular exponentiation problem
nodes.statement: Given $n$, $x$, and $r$, compute $x^r \bmod n$. The bottleneck of the quantum factoring algorithm.

nodes.name: Quantum Fourier transform $A_q$
nodes.statement: The unitary $A_q$ with $(a,c)$ entry $\frac{1}{q^{1/2}} \exp(2\pi i ac/q)$, sending $\|a\rangle \mapsto \frac{1}{q^{1/2}} \sum_{c=0}^{q-1} \exp(2\pi i ac/q) \|c\rangle$.

nodes.name: Order of an element mod $n$
nodes.statement: The order of $x$ in the multiplicative group $\bmod n$ is the least positive integer $r$ such that $x^r \equiv 1 \bmod n$.

nodes.name: Discrete logarithm
nodes.statement: Given a prime $p$ and a generator $g$ of the multiplicative group $\bmod p$, the discrete logarithm of $x$ is the integer $r$ with $0 \leq r < p-1$ such that $g^r \equiv x \bmod p$.

nodes.name: Quantum watchdog (Zeno) effect
nodes.statement: Repeatedly measuring an intermediate register that should equal $0$ collapses any erroneous amplitude back onto the desired state, potentially stabilizing the quantum computation.

nodes.name: Integer factorization
nodes.statement: Given a composite integer $n$, output a non-trivial factor of $n$. Believed hard classically; underlies RSA cryptography.

nodes.name: Order finding mod $n$
nodes.statement: Given $x$ and $n$ with $\gcd(x,n)=1$, find the least $r \geq 1$ with $x^r \equiv 1 \bmod n$.

nodes.name: Discrete logarithm mod $p$
nodes.statement: Given a prime $p$, generator $g$ of $(\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^*$, and $x$, find $r$ with $g^r \equiv x \bmod p$.

nodes.name: Universality of two-bit gates
nodes.statement: Any unitary transformation on $n$ bits can be expressed as a composition of two-bit unitary gates; in particular, all one-bit gates together with the controlled-NOT form a universal set for quantum computation.
assumptions: Gates act on a Hilbert space of dimension $2^n$
conclusions: Any $n$-bit unitary decomposes into one-bit gates and controlled-NOTs
nodes.origin_citation: DiVincenzo 1995; Sleator and Weinfurter 1995; Lloyd 1995; Deutsch et al. 1995

nodes.name: Reversible simulation of classical computation
nodes.statement: Any deterministic polynomial-time computation can be performed by a reversible gate array with only constant-factor overhead in time.
assumptions: A classical algorithm runs in time $T$
conclusions: A reversible gate array exists with running time $O(T)$

nodes.name: Reduction of factoring to order finding
nodes.statement: If $n$ is odd and not a prime power with $k$ distinct odd prime factors, then for a random $x \bmod n$, computing $\gcd(x^{r/2}-1, n)$ where $r$ is the order of $x$ yields a non-trivial factor of $n$ with probability at least $1 - 1/2^{k-1}$.
assumptions: $n$ is odd, composite, and not a prime power
$x$ is chosen uniformly at random from $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^*$
conclusions: $\Pr[\gcd(x^{r/2}-1,n) \text{ is a non-trivial factor of } n] \geq 1 - 1/2^{k-1}$

nodes.name: Chinese remainder theorem
nodes.statement: If $n = \prod_i p_i^{a_i}$, then choosing $x \bmod n$ uniformly at random is equivalent to independently choosing $x_i \bmod p_i^{a_i}$ uniformly at random for each $i$.

nodes.name: Cyclicity of $(\mathbb{Z}/p^\alpha\mathbb{Z})^*$
nodes.statement: For every odd prime power $p^\alpha$, the multiplicative group $(\mathbb{Z}/p^\alpha\mathbb{Z})^*$ is cyclic.

nodes.name: Lower bound on Euler totient
nodes.statement: There exists a constant $\delta>0$ such that $\phi(r)/r > \delta/\log\log r$ for all $r \geq 3$.

nodes.name: Correctness of quantum order-finding
nodes.statement: The quantum order-finding algorithm finds the order $r$ of $x \bmod n$ in time $O((\log n)^2 (\log \log n)(\log \log \log n))$ with high probability after $O(\log \log r)$ repetitions.
assumptions: $q$ is the power of $2$ with $n^2 \leq q < 2n^2$
conclusions: The algorithm outputs $r$ with probability $\geq \delta/\log\log r$ per trial
Total running time is $O((\log n)^2 (\log \log n)(\log \log \log n))$

nodes.name: Polynomial-time quantum factoring
nodes.statement: There is a quantum algorithm that factors an integer $n$ in time $O((\log n)^2 (\log \log n)(\log \log \log n))$ with bounded error probability.
assumptions: $n$ is a composite integer with $k \geq 2$ distinct odd prime factors
conclusions: A non-trivial factor of $n$ is output with high probability in quantum polynomial time

nodes.name: Polynomial-time quantum discrete logarithm
nodes.statement: There is a quantum algorithm using two modular exponentiations and two quantum Fourier transforms that finds the discrete logarithm of $x$ to base $g$ modulo a prime $p$ in polynomial time with bounded error probability.
conclusions: The discrete logarithm $r$ with $g^r \equiv x \bmod p$ is found in $\mathrm{poly}(\log p)$ quantum time with high probability

nodes.name: Lower bound on order-finding observation probability
nodes.statement: For each $k$ with $0 \leq k < r$, the probability of observing a state $\|c, x^k \bmod n\rangle$ with $|\langle rc \rangle_q| \leq r/2$ is at least $4/(\pi^2 r^2) \geq 1/(3r^2)$ for sufficiently large $n$.
assumptions: $q$ is a power of $2$ with $n^2 \leq q < 2n^2$

nodes.name: Continued-fraction recovery of $d/r$
nodes.statement: Since $q > n^2$, there is at most one fraction $d/r$ with $r < n$ satisfying $|c/q - d/r| \leq 1/(2q)$, and it is recoverable in polynomial time by continued-fraction expansion of $c/q$.
conclusions: $d/r$ is unique and computable in $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ time

nodes.name: Probability of good output (discrete log)
nodes.statement: For each pair $(c,d)$ satisfying conditions (\ref{firstcond}) and (\ref{secondcond}), the probability of observing some good state $\|c,d,y\rangle$ is at least $0.054/q^2 > 1/(20q^2)$.

nodes.name: Count of good $(c,d)$ pairs
nodes.statement: The number of good pairs $(c,d)$ satisfying both conditions is at least $q/12$, hence the probability of observing some good state is at least $p/(240q) \geq 1/480$.
conclusions: Number of good pairs is $\geq q/12$
Total probability of a good state $\geq 1/480$

nodes.name: Recovering $r$ from good $c'$ samples
nodes.statement: After $O(t)$ experiments yielding $t$ good $c'$ values, with constant probability every prime power $p_i^{\alpha_i} > 18$ dividing $p-1$ is coprime to at least one of these $c'$'s, allowing $r \bmod p_i^{\alpha_i}$ to be recovered.
assumptions: Each good $c'$ is generated with probability $\geq 1/(40q)$
conclusions: A sufficient sample size $t = O(1)$ recovers $r$ modulo all prime powers $> 18$ dividing $p-1$ with probability $\geq 1/2$

nodes.name: Quantum Fourier transform action
nodes.statement: $\|a\rangle \mapsto \frac{1}{q^{1/2}} \sum_{c=0}^{q-1} \|c\rangle \exp(2\pi i ac/q)$.

nodes.name: QFT gate sequence
nodes.statement: $R_{l-1} S_{l-2,l-1} R_{l-2} S_{l-3,l-1} S_{l-3,l-2} R_{l-3} \ldots R_1 S_{0,l-1} \ldots S_{0,1} R_0$, requiring $l(l-1)/2$ gates for $q = 2^l$.

nodes.name: Order-finding observation probability
nodes.statement: $\Pr[\|c, x^k \bmod n\rangle] = \left| \frac{1}{q} \sum_{b=0}^{\lfloor (q-k-1)/r \rfloor} \exp(2\pi i b \langle rc \rangle_q / q) \right|^2$.

nodes.name: Diophantine condition for order finding
nodes.statement: $\left| \frac{c}{q} - \frac{d}{r} \right| \leq \frac{1}{2q}$.

nodes.name: Reversible modular exponentiation
nodes.statement: Reversible gate array that computes $(a, x^a \bmod n)$ from $a$ in $O(l^3)$ time and $O(l)$ space, where $l = \lceil \log_2 n \rceil$.
input: Fixed integers $x$ and $n$ built into gate structure
nodes.pseudocode: power := 1; for i = 0 to l-1: if a_i == 1 then power := power * x^{2^i} mod n

nodes.name: Quantum Fourier transform (Coppersmith / Deutsch construction)
nodes.statement: Polynomial-time quantum circuit for $A_q$ when $q = 2^l$, built from one-bit Hadamard-like gates $R_j$ and two-bit conditional-phase gates $S_{j,k}$, using $l(l-1)/2$ gates total.

nodes.name: Quantum order-finding algorithm
nodes.statement: Quantum algorithm that finds the order $r$ of $x \bmod n$ using one modular exponentiation, one quantum Fourier transform, and classical continued-fraction post-processing.

nodes.name: Shor's quantum factoring algorithm
nodes.statement: Quantum algorithm that factors a composite $n$ by sampling random $x$, calling the order-finding subroutine, and computing $\gcd(x^{r/2}\pm 1, n)$.
input: Composite odd integer $n$ that is not a prime power

nodes.name: Shor's quantum discrete logarithm algorithm
nodes.statement: Quantum algorithm using two modular exponentiations and two QFTs to find $r$ such that $g^r \equiv x \bmod p$, with classical post-processing via the Chinese remainder theorem.

nodes.name: Schoenhage-Strassen multiplication
nodes.statement: FFT-based gate array for integer multiplication that uses $O(l \log l \log \log l)$ gates to multiply two $l$-bit numbers.

nodes.name: Bennett's reversibility transformation
nodes.statement: Procedure that turns any non-reversible gate array for $F$ into a reversible gate array computing $x \mapsto F(x)$, using extra workspace and a record register that is uncomputed at the end.
output: Reversible gate array computing $F$ (and erasing $x$ when $F^{-1}$ is also available)

nodes.name: Number field sieve
nodes.statement: Best known classical factoring algorithm, with running time $\exp(c (\log n)^{1/3} (\log \log n)^{2/3})$.

nodes.name: Two-bit quantum gate truth table
nodes.statement: Example gate sending $\|00\rangle \to \|00\rangle$, $\|01\rangle \to \|01\rangle$, $\|10\rangle \to \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\|10\rangle + \|11\rangle)$, $\|11\rangle \to \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}(\|10\rangle - \|11\rangle)$, illustrating quantum interference.

nodes.name: Order-finding probability plot ($r=10$, $q=256$)
nodes.statement: Plot of $\Pr(c)$ for the order-finding algorithm with $r = 10$ and $q = 256$ (which would arise when factoring $33$ with $x = 5$); peaks occur near integer multiples of $q/r = 256/10$.

nodes.name: Approximate Fourier transform suffices
nodes.statement: Coppersmith [1994] showed that ignoring the small phase factors $S_{j,k}$ with large $k-j$ yields an approximate QFT that still works for factoring while reducing gate count.

nodes.name: Algorithm generalizes beyond multiplication mod $n$
nodes.statement: The order-finding algorithm works for any permutation $f$ on $\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ whose $k$-th iterate $f^{(k)}(a)$ is computable in time $\mathrm{poly}(\log n, \log k)$.

nodes.name: Generalization to abelian groups
nodes.statement: Boneh and Lipton [1995] generalized the discrete-log algorithm so it can find discrete logarithms when the group is abelian but not cyclic.

nodes.name: Precision and decoherence requirements
nodes.statement: Bennett et al. [1994] showed that quantum gates need precision only $O(1/t)$ and decoherence only polynomially small in $t$ to complete $t$ steps with reasonable success probability.

nodes.name: Quantum algorithms for NP-complete problems
nodes.statement: Are there polynomial-time quantum algorithms for NP-complete problems? Some weak evidence suggests not, but the question is open.

nodes.name: Quantum algorithm for short lattice vectors
nodes.statement: Is there a quantum polynomial-time algorithm for finding a short vector in a lattice? This problem is not known to be NP-complete and may be amenable to quantum techniques.

nodes.name: Quantum speedup of integer multiplication
nodes.statement: Can integer multiplication itself be sped up by a quantum algorithm? An affirmative answer would yield faster factoring (potentially faster than classical RSA encryption).

nodes.name: Proof of factoring/order-finding reduction
nodes.statement: Use the Chinese remainder theorem to factor the random choice into independent components mod each $p_i^{a_i}$; the algorithm fails only if all the largest powers of $2$ dividing the local orders agree, an event of probability at most $1/2^{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of QFT correctness
nodes.statement: Track the phase contributions of $R_j$ and $S_{j,k}$ along each path $\|a\rangle \to \|b\rangle$, sum over $0 \le j \le k < l$, change variables to recover the phase $2\pi ac/q$, matching the target unitary.

nodes.name: Proof of order-finding probability bound
nodes.statement: Bound the probability $|\frac{1}{q}\sum_b \exp(2\pi i b \langle rc\rangle_q/q)|^2$ by approximating the sum with an integral; the integral is minimized at $|\langle rc\rangle_q|/r = 1/2$ giving value $\geq 4/(\pi^2 r^2)$.

nodes.name: Proof of order-finding correctness
nodes.statement: Combine the per-state probability bound (Lemma LP317.1) with the count of $r\phi(r)$ recoverable states and the Hardy-Wright bound on $\phi(r)/r$ to conclude that $O(\log\log r)$ trials suffice.

nodes.name: Proof of discrete-log algorithm correctness
nodes.statement: Classify outputs as good/bad via conditions on $\langle T\rangle_q$ and $\langle c(p-1)\rangle_q$; show good outputs occur with constant probability and yield $r \bmod p_i^{\alpha_i}$ for primes $p_i > 18$, then handle small primes by enumeration via the Chinese remainder theorem.

nodes.name: Set up via CRT decomposition
nodes.statement: Write $n = \prod_{i=1}^{k} p_i^{a_i}$. Let $r_i$ be the order of $x \bmod p_i^{a_i}$, so $r$ is the least common multiple of the $r_i$.

nodes.name: Identify failure conditions
nodes.statement: The algorithm fails only if all the largest powers of $2$ dividing the $r_i$ agree (then either $r$ is odd or $x^{r/2} \equiv -1 \bmod n$).

nodes.name: Bound failure probability
nodes.statement: By cyclicity of $(\mathbb{Z}/p^\alpha\mathbb{Z})^*$, each $r_i$'s 2-adic valuation matches a fixed value with probability $\leq 1/2$, so all $k$ agree with probability $\leq 1/2^{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Conclude success probability
nodes.statement: Therefore the procedure outputs a non-trivial factor of $n$ with probability $\geq 1 - 1/2^{k-1}$.

nodes.name: Account for $1/\sqrt 2$ normalizations
nodes.statement: The $l$ factors of $1/\sqrt 2$ from the $R$ matrices multiply to give the global factor $1/q^{1/2}$, matching the target.

nodes.name: Sum phase contributions per path
nodes.statement: On the unique path from $\|a\rangle$ to $\|b\rangle$, the phase is $\sum_{0\leq j<l} \pi a_j b_j + \sum_{0\leq j<k<l} \frac{\pi}{2^{k-j}} a_j b_k$.

nodes.name: Substitute bit-reversal $c \leftrightarrow b$
nodes.statement: Use $b_k = c_{l-1-k}$ and the substitution $k \to l-k-1$ to rewrite the phase as $\sum_{0 \leq j+k < l} 2\pi \frac{2^j 2^k}{2^l} a_j c_k$.

nodes.name: Identify total phase $2\pi ac/q$
nodes.statement: Extending the sum to all $j,k < l$ (extra terms are multiples of $2\pi$) and using distributivity yields phase $\frac{2\pi}{q} ac$, matching the QFT.

nodes.name: Approximate sum by integral
nodes.statement: Replace $\frac{1}{q}\sum_{b=0}^{\lfloor (q-k-1)/r\rfloor} \exp(2\pi i b \langle rc\rangle_q/q)$ with an integral, with error term $O(1/q)$ when $|\langle rc\rangle_q| \leq r/2$.

nodes.name: Substitute $u = rb/q$
nodes.statement: After substitution, the integral becomes $\frac{1}{r} \int_0^1 \exp(2\pi i \frac{\langle rc\rangle_q}{r} u)\, du$ up to $O(1/q)$ error.

nodes.name: Minimize over $\langle rc\rangle_q/r$
nodes.statement: Letting $\langle rc\rangle_q/r \in [-1/2, 1/2]$, the absolute integral is minimized at $\pm 1/2$ with value $2/(\pi r)$, hence the probability is $\geq 4/(\pi^2 r^2) \geq 1/(3r^2)$.

nodes.name: Translate good $c$ to Diophantine condition
nodes.statement: $|\langle rc\rangle_q| \leq r/2$ rearranges to $|c/q - d/r| \leq 1/(2q)$ for some $d$.

nodes.name: Recover $d/r$ via continued fractions
nodes.statement: Since $q > n^2$, the fraction $d/r$ with $r < n$ is unique and is found by continued-fraction expansion of $c/q$.

nodes.name: Count recoverable states
nodes.statement: There are $\phi(r)$ values of $d$ coprime to $r$ and $r$ values of $x^k$, giving $r\phi(r)$ states $\|c, x^k\rangle$ from which $r$ can be recovered, total probability $\geq \phi(r)/(3r)$.

nodes.name: Apply Hardy-Wright bound
nodes.statement: Using $\phi(r)/r > \delta/\log\log r$, $O(\log\log r)$ repetitions of the experiment suffice to find $r$ with high probability.

nodes.name: Define good outputs
nodes.statement: Call $(c,d,y)$ good if $|\langle rc + d - \frac{r}{p-1}\langle c(p-1)\rangle_q\rangle_q| \leq 1/2$ and $|\langle c(p-1)\rangle_q| \leq q/12$.

nodes.name: Lower-bound good-state probability
nodes.statement: For each good $(c,d)$ pair, the amplitude has magnitude $\geq \frac{2}{q} \int_0^{1/2} \cos(\pi/6 + 2\pi |W| u)\, du$, giving probability $\geq 0.054/q^2 > 1/(20q^2)$.

nodes.name: Count good pairs and overall probability
nodes.statement: There are $\geq q/12$ good $(c,d)$ pairs and $p-1$ values of $y$, giving total good-state probability $\geq p/(240q) \geq 1/480$.

nodes.name: Recover $r$ for prime powers $> 18$
nodes.statement: After $O(t)$ trials, with probability $\geq 1/2$ every prime power $p_i^{\alpha_i} > 18$ dividing $p-1$ is coprime to some sampled $c'$, allowing $r \bmod p_i^{\alpha_i}$ to be computed.

nodes.name: Handle small primes and combine via CRT
nodes.statement: Enumerate residues modulo prime powers $\leq 18$, then use the Chinese remainder theorem to assemble $r$ and verify by computing $g^r \bmod p$.

nodes.name: Choose $q$ and prepare uniform superposition
nodes.statement: Find $q$ a power of $2$ with $n^2 \leq q < 2n^2$. Initialize the first register to $\frac{1}{q^{1/2}} \sum_{a=0}^{q-1} \|a\rangle\|0\rangle$ by Hadamard-like operations on each bit.

nodes.name: Compute $x^a \bmod n$ in second register
nodes.statement: Apply reversible modular exponentiation to map $\|a\rangle\|0\rangle$ to $\|a\rangle\|x^a \bmod n\rangle$.

nodes.name: Apply QFT $A_q$ to first register
nodes.statement: Apply the quantum Fourier transform $A_q$ to the first register, producing $\frac{1}{q} \sum_{a,c} \exp(2\pi i ac/q) \|c\rangle\|x^a \bmod n\rangle$.

nodes.name: Measure registers
nodes.statement: Observe both registers, obtaining a sample $(c, x^k \bmod n)$ with the order-finding probability distribution.

nodes.name: Continued-fraction post-processing
nodes.statement: Round $c/q$ to the nearest fraction $d/r$ with denominator $< n$ via continued-fraction expansion; output the candidate $r$.

nodes.name: Sample random $x \bmod n$
nodes.statement: Pick $x$ uniformly at random in $\{2, \ldots, n-1\}$; if $\gcd(x,n) > 1$ return that gcd as a non-trivial factor.

nodes.name: Find order $r$ via quantum subroutine
nodes.statement: Invoke the quantum order-finding algorithm to obtain $r$ such that $x^r \equiv 1 \bmod n$.

nodes.name: Test $r$ and compute gcd
nodes.statement: If $r$ is odd or $x^{r/2} \equiv -1 \bmod n$, restart; otherwise output $\gcd(x^{r/2} \pm 1, n)$ as a non-trivial factor.

nodes.name: Choose $q$ close to $p$
nodes.statement: Find $q$ a power of $2$ with $p < q < 2p$.

nodes.name: Prepare two-register superposition and compute $g^a x^{-b} \bmod p$
nodes.statement: Put first two registers in uniform superposition over $\|a\rangle\|b\rangle$ for $a, b \in \{0, \ldots, p-2\}$, and compute $g^a x^{-b} \bmod p$ in the third register.

nodes.name: Apply QFT $A_q$ to both first registers
nodes.statement: Apply $A_q$ to each of the first two registers, sending $\|a,b\rangle \to \frac{1}{q}\sum_{c,d} \exp(2\pi i (ac+bd)/q)\|c,d\rangle$.

nodes.name: Measure all three registers
nodes.statement: Observe the state to obtain $(c, d, y = g^k \bmod p)$.

nodes.name: Recover $r$ via CRT post-processing
nodes.statement: Round $d/q$ to the nearest multiple of $1/(p-1)$ and divide by $c' = (c(p-1) - \langle c(p-1)\rangle_q)/q$; combine residues from multiple trials via the Chinese remainder theorem to recover $r$.
